name: Haile Gebrselassie
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 5000m and 10000m at the 1992 World Junior Championships in Seoul at age 19, then won senior World Championship gold in the 10000m at age 20 in 1993.
early_history_summary: Born into poverty in rural Asella, Ethiopia, Haile ran 10km to school and back daily from childhood, building enormous aerobic capacity at altitude. He was inspired by Ethiopian Olympic champion Miruts Yifter and began formal athletics training in his mid-teens, joining an athletics club in Addis Ababa with his brother around age 15. His international breakthrough came at the 1992 World Junior Championships.
family_context_summary: Born one of ten children to a subsistence farmer father in Asella, Arsi Province, Ethiopia; mother died of cancer when Haile was six. The family lived in a single-room wooden house in extreme poverty.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in athletics; father was a subsistence farmer who initially opposed Haile's running. An older brother also ran, which helped Haile get started.
primary_early_advantage_tags: altitude conditioning, daily running, poverty-driven, Ethiopian running tradition, natural physique
evidence_summary: Haile Gebrselassie grew up in extreme poverty in the Arsi highlands of Ethiopia, running 10km to school daily at altitude, which built exceptional aerobic capacity from childhood. His father was a subsistence farmer with no athletics background, but the Arsi region's high altitude and Ethiopia's distance-running tradition provided a natural performance pipeline. He won World Junior titles at 19 and senior World Championship gold at 20, driven by physical talent, daily running reps, and the urgency of escaping poverty. No financial safety net or family domain advantage was present; his advantage was geographic (altitude), physical (natural distance-running physique), and motivational (poverty as catalyst).
starting_point: Born into extreme poverty in rural Asella, Arsi Province, Ethiopia; father was a subsistence farmer, mother died when he was six; family of ten children in a single-room house.
current_position: Retired from competitive running in 2015; successful businessman with interests in real estate, car dealership, and a cinema in Addis Ababa; estimated net worth in the tens of millions of dollars; resides in Ethiopia.

trajectory.event: Won 5000m and 10000m gold at the World Junior Championships in Seoul, gaining international recognition.
Won senior World Championship gold in the 10000m at Stuttgart, plus silver in the 5000m.
Set his first world record in the 5000m (12:56.96), breaking Said Aouita's mark.
Won Olympic gold in the 10000m at the Atlanta Olympics.
Won second consecutive Olympic gold in the 10000m at the Sydney Olympics.
Broke the marathon world record in Berlin (2:04:26).
Retired from competitive running after a career spanning over two decades.

name: Ding Junhui
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Asian Under-21 Championship, the Asian Championship, and the IBSF World Under-21 Championship in 2002 at age 15, becoming the youngest ever winner of the IBSF World Under-21 title.
early_history_summary: Ding began playing snooker at age eight at a billiard hall near his home in Yixing, Jiangsu Province, where his father was a snooker enthusiast. His father recognized his talent, opened a snooker club, then sold the family's grocery business and house to move to Dongguan, Guangdong Province, where Ding practiced eight hours a day. Ding quit formal education at age 11 to focus entirely on snooker.
family_context_summary: Born to Ding Wenjun, a snooker player and grocery store owner, and Chen Xijuan in Yixing, Jiangsu Province. The family sold their house and business and went into debt to fund Ding's snooker training, eventually moving to Dongguan for better coaching opportunities.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Ding Wenjun was a snooker player who recognized his son's talent at age eight, opened a snooker club to ensure practice access, and made extraordinary financial sacrifices including selling the family home to fund Ding's training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father snooker player, sold house, quit school, 8 hours daily practice, Dongguan training hub
evidence_summary: Ding Junhui's father, a snooker player himself, recognized his son's talent at age eight and made extraordinary sacrifices: opening a snooker club, selling the family home and grocery business, and moving to Dongguan so Ding could train at the national team's training center. Ding quit school at 11 to practice eight hours daily, accumulating exceptional reps before his milestone. The family went into severe debt and lived in a tiny partitioned room in a snooker club. This family-domain apprenticeship, combined with extreme concentration and adversity (total family financial sacrifice), propelled Ding to become Asian and World Under-21 champion at 15.
starting_point: Born in Yixing, Jiangsu Province, China to a grocery store owner and snooker enthusiast father and a mother who initially opposed the focus on snooker; family was lower-middle-class before selling everything for Ding's training.
current_position: Active professional snooker player ranked approximately 15th in the world as of 2026; has won 15 ranking titles including three UK Championships; resides in the United Kingdom and China.

trajectory.event: Won the Asian Under-21 Championship, Asian Championship, and IBSF World Under-21 Championship, becoming the youngest ever IBSF World Under-21 winner.
Turned professional on the main snooker tour via WPBTSA concession.
Won the China Open and UK Championship, becoming the first player from outside Great Britain and Ireland to win the UK Championship.
Reached world number one ranking in December 2014.
Became the first Asian player to reach the World Snooker Championship final at the Crucible.

name: Lyudmila Ulitskaya
milestone_by_age_26: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 found. Ulitskaya's literary career began in 1979 (age 36) with the Jewish drama theatre; her first published fiction appeared in 1990 (age 47) and her breakthrough novel Sonechka in 1992 (age 49).
early_history_summary: Born in Davlekanovo, Bashkiria during WWII evacuation; family moved to Moscow when she was an infant. She earned a degree in genetics from Moscow State University and worked at the Institute of General Genetics from 1968-1970 before being fired for distributing samizdat literature. She then spent about nine years without formal employment before joining the Hebrew Theatre of Moscow as a literary consultant in 1979.
family_context_summary: Born to a family evacuated during WWII; raised in communal apartments in Moscow. Family background details beyond this are not well documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Lyudmila Ulitskaya did not achieve literary recognition until her late forties. She trained as a geneticist, was fired for samizdat distribution in 1970, and only began her literary career in 1979 at the Hebrew Theatre of Moscow. Her first published fiction appeared in 1990 and her breakthrough novel Sonechka in 1992. No material milestone by age 26 (~1969) was found in reviewed sources.

name: Vadym Gutzeit
milestone_by_age_26: Won the World Junior Sabre Championship in 1989 at age 18 and again in 1990 at age 19, then won Olympic team sabre gold at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics at age 20.
early_history_summary: Gutzeit took up fencing at age nine under coach Alexander Obolensky. He won the Ukrainian national sabre championship at age 15 and became USSR Junior Sabre Champion in 1988 at age 16-17. He fenced for Dynamo Kiev, a major Soviet sports club, and rapidly ascended through the Soviet fencing pipeline to become world junior champion and Olympic champion before age 21.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Gutzeit grew up in Kiev, Ukraine (then part of the Soviet Union) and trained within the Soviet sports system.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet sports system, Dynamo Kiev, early fencing start, Obolensky coaching
evidence_summary: Vadym Gutzeit benefited from the elite Soviet sports pipeline, starting fencing at age nine under coach Alexander Obolensky and training at Dynamo Kiev, a major state-sponsored sports club. He won the Ukrainian national championship at 15 and became World Junior Sabre Champion at 18, demonstrating early specialization within a structured institutional system. No family financial or domain advantage was documented; his advantage was primarily institutional — access to the Soviet fencing infrastructure and coaching. He won Olympic team gold at 20, completing the pipeline from junior to senior elite level.
starting_point: Born in Kiev, Ukrainian SSR, Soviet Union; family background not documented in reviewed sources; trained within the Soviet state sports system from age nine.
current_position: President of the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine; served as Ukraine's Youth and Sport Minister from 2020 to 2023; resides in Ukraine.

trajectory.event: Won gold medal in the Junior Under-20 Sabre World Fencing Championships.

name: Cabu
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded the satirical magazine Hara-Kiri in 1960 at age 22, which became the predecessor to Charlie Hebdo and a landmark in French satirical journalism.
early_history_summary: Born Jean Maurice Jules Cabut in Châlons-sur-Marne, France to a professor father who was an amateur painter. He won a drawing contest at age 14 and began publishing drawings in the daily newspaper L'Union at age 15. He left school at 16 to apprentice at a printing workshop in Paris while attending the École Estienne and Académie Julian. After conscription in the Algerian War (1958-60), he co-founded Hara-Kiri in 1960.
family_context_summary: Born to a petite bourgeoisie Catholic family in Châlons-sur-Marne. Father Marcel Cabut was a professor at the École nationale supérieure d'arts et métiers and an amateur painter who encouraged artistic interests.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a professor at a national arts school and an amateur painter, providing early exposure to drawing and visual arts. The family valued education and artistic expression.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father painter, early publishing, art school, Paris press scene, Hara-Kiri founding
evidence_summary: Cabu grew up in a petite bourgeoisie family in Châlons-sur-Marne with a father who was a professor at a national arts school and an amateur painter, providing early exposure to visual arts. He won a drawing contest at 14 and began publishing in a daily newspaper at 15, demonstrating early domain immersion. He moved to Paris at 16 to attend art school (École Estienne, Académie Julian) and apprentice at a printing workshop. His conscription during the Algerian War shaped his anti-militarist artistic voice. At 22, he co-founded Hara-Kiri, a landmark satirical magazine, alongside collaborators like Cavanna, Bernier, and Wolinski.
starting_point: Born in Châlons-sur-Marne, France to a petite bourgeoisie Catholic family; father was a professor at the École nationale supérieure d'arts et métiers and an amateur painter.
current_position: Died on 7 January 2015 at age 76 in Paris, murdered in the Charlie Hebdo terrorist attack; final role: staff cartoonist and shareholder at Charlie Hebdo.

trajectory.event: First drawings published in the daily newspaper L'Union in Reims, beginning a professional publishing career.
Co-founded the satirical magazine Hara-Kiri with François Cavanna, Georges Bernier, and others, a landmark in French satirical journalism.
Joined Pilote magazine, where he developed the character Grand Duduche based on his school memories.
Became a founding contributor to Charlie Hebdo after Hara-Kiri was banned.
Joined Le Canard enchaîné as a regular contributor, expanding his reach in French political satire.
Murdered in the Charlie Hebdo terrorist attack in Paris on 7 January 2015.

name: Lin Dan
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Asian Junior Championships in 2000 at age 17, then achieved world number one ranking and won the All England Open title in 2004 at age 20, the youngest men's singles player to reach number one.
early_history_summary: Born in Longyan, Fujian, China to sports-enthusiast parents. He started badminton training at age five under family friend and coach Chen Weihua. At age 12, after winning the National Junior Championships, he was scouted by the People's Liberation Army Sports Team. He entered the Chinese National Badminton Team in 2001 at age 18 and quickly rose to international prominence, reaching world number one by February 2004.
family_context_summary: Born in Longyan, Fujian to parents who were both sports enthusiasts. Father Lin Jianbin worked at a transport company and mother Gao Xiuyu worked at a pharmaceutical company. The family was middle-class; parents were sent-down youth during the Cultural Revolution who settled in Shanghang County.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were sports enthusiasts (father played volleyball and basketball, mother played basketball and swam) but not professional athletes. A family friend, Chen Weihua, was a local badminton coach who introduced Lin to the sport at age five and later facilitated his entry into the PLA Sports Team.
primary_early_advantage_tags: PLA Sports Team, Chinese national team, Fujian badminton, coach Chen Weihua, started at age 5
evidence_summary: Lin Dan benefited from China's elite badminton pipeline: starting training at age five under a family friend who was a local coach, being scouted by the PLA Sports Team at 12 after winning National Junior Championships, and entering the Chinese National Badminton Team at 18. His parents were sports enthusiasts but not professionals; the family was middle-class. The institutional pipeline (PLA → National Team) concentrated opportunity and provided elite coaching, facilities, and peer competition. By 20, he was world number one and All England champion, completing the pipeline from junior to senior elite level with exceptional accumulated reps from 13 years of training.
starting_point: Born in Longyan, Fujian, China to middle-class parents; father worked at a transport company and mother at a pharmaceutical company; both parents were sports enthusiasts who settled in Shanghang County after being sent-down youth during the Cultural Revolution.
current_position: Retired from professional badminton in July 2020; widely regarded as the greatest badminton player of all time; inducted into BWF Hall of Fame in 2023; resides in China.

trajectory.event: Won the Asian Junior Championships in both team and singles events, marking his emergence on the international stage.
Enlisted into the Chinese National Badminton Team, beginning his senior professional career.
Achieved world number one ranking for the first time (February 26) and won his first All England Open title.

Won Olympic gold in men's singles at the Beijing Olympics.
Defended Olympic gold at the London Olympics, becoming the first men's singles player to win back-to-back Olympic titles.
Announced retirement from professional badminton, finishing with 66 career titles.
Inducted into the BWF Badminton Hall of Fame.

name: Reine Wisell
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Swedish Formula 3 Championship in 1967 at age 25, establishing himself as a top emerging racing driver in Sweden's competitive F3 scene.
early_history_summary: Born in Motala, Sweden. He began racing in saloon cars in 1962 at age 20-21 with a Ford Anglia and Mini Cooper. He switched to Formula 3 in 1966 with a Cooper T76, and in 1967 won the Swedish F3 Championship with a Brabham BT18. He progressed to Formula 5000 and made his Formula One debut in 1970 with Team Lotus, finishing third at the US Grand Prix on his debut.
family_context_summary: Born in the small lakeside town of Motala, Sweden. Family financial and professional background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Swedish F3 scene, bought own cars, Ronnie Peterson rivalry, saloon car start
evidence_summary: Reine Wisell began racing relatively late at age 20-21 in 1962 with saloon cars, buying his own vehicles. He progressed to Formula 3 in 1966 and won the Swedish F3 Championship in 1967 at age 25, benefiting from Sweden's thriving F3 scene and his rivalry with fellow Swede Ronnie Peterson. No family financial or domain advantage was documented; he self-created his racing career by purchasing cars and competing in the Swedish national scene. His F1 debut came at 29 with Team Lotus, where he achieved a remarkable third-place finish.
starting_point: Born in the small lakeside town of Motala, Sweden; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died on 20 March 2022 at age 80 in Pattaya, Thailand; final racing career spanned F1 (1970-1974) with Lotus, BRM, and March teams, followed by decades in GT, sports, and historic racing.
